{{short description|Non-periodic tiling of space by prisms}}
[[Image:Quaquaversal Tiling.svg|200px|thumb|The substitution rule for the quaquaversal tiling.]]

In [[geometry]], the '''quaquaversal tiling''' is a [[aperiodic tiling|nonperiodic tiling]] of Euclidean 3-space introduced by [[John Horton Conway|John Conway]] and [[Charles Radin]]. It is analogous to the [[pinwheel tiling]] in 2 dimensions having tile orientations that are dense in {{math|[[SO(3)]]}}. The basic solid tiles are [[30-60-90]] [[triangular prism]]s arranged in a pattern such that some copies are rotated by {{math|π/3}}, and some are rotated by {{math|π/2}} in a perpendicular direction.{{r|cr}}

They construct the group {{math|G(''p'',''q'')}} given by a rotation of {{math|2π/''p''}} and a perpendicular rotation by {{math|2π/''q''}}; the orientations in the quaquaversal tiling are given by {{math|G(6,4)}}. {{math|G(''p'',1)}} are [[cyclic group]]s, {{math|G(''p'',2)}} are [[dihedral group]]s, {{math|G(4,4)}} is the [[octahedral group]], and all other {{math|G(''p'',''q'')}} are infinite and dense in {{math|SO(3)}}; if {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} are odd and ≥3, then {{math|G(''p'',''q'')}} is a [[free group]].{{r|cr}}

Radin and Lorenzo Sadun constructed similar honeycombs based on a tiling related to the [[Penrose tilings]] and the pinwheel tiling; the former has orientations in {{math|G(10,4)}}, and the latter has orientations in {{math|G(''p'',4)}} with the irrational rotation {{math|1=2π/''p'' = arctan(1/2)}}. They show that {{math|G(''p'',4)}} is dense in {{math|SO(3)}} for the aforementioned value of {{mvar|p}}, and whenever {{math|cos(2π/''p'')}} is [[transcendental number|transcendental]].{{r|r}}
